case_info.scenario: A 53-year-old woman with a history of stage IVA1 (T4N1M0B2) mycosis fungoides presented with a new 1-month history of hyperpigmentation of the oral mucosa (Figure 1). Examination of the mouth revealed multiple coalescing painless nonpruritic black macules and patches on the tongue, roof of the mouth, and buccal mucosa. Examination of the skin was notable for erythematous and hyperpigmented patches covering 90% of the body surface area, consistent with her known mycosis fungoides. Other notable findings on examination were 1- to 2-cm lymphadenopathy in the bilateral inguinal folds and axillae. Review of systems was notable for fatigue. The patient had previously received 5 cycles of romidepsin with progression of disease, followed by 4 doses of pegylated liposomal doxorubicin hydrochloride, which was followed by partial response.
case_info.caption: Black macules and patches on the tongue, roof of the mouth, and buccal mucosa.
case_info.explanation: Oral hyperpigmentation is a rare adverse effect of certain chemotherapy agents, such as doxorubicin. The exact mechanism of this phenomenon is not well understood. One hypothesis is that chemotherapy drugs can trigger increased melanin deposition in the oral mucosa. The risk is thought to be higher in individuals of African descent.1,2However, this adverse effect is underreported, and it is important for treating physicians to be familiar with this adverse effect to avoid unnecessary testing and undue stress to the patient. Doxorubicin is an anthracycline-based chemotherapy that is frequently used as a single agent or in combination therapy to treat various types of cancer, such as breast cancer, multiple myeloma, and non-Hodgkin lymphoma.3Doxorubicin directly inhibits topoisomerase II, thereby preventing DNA synthesis.3There are several formulations, including pegylated liposomal doxorubicin and nonliposomal conventional formulations.3Single-agent pegylated liposomal doxorubicin is typically used for treatment of advanced mycosis fungoides.4Although this is often an effective treatment option in cases of refractory and recalcitrant mycosis fungoides, it is also associated with several oral adverse effects, including mucositis, altered taste, and oral hyperpigmentation.5 Doxorubicin-induced oral hyperpigmentation is a rare adverse effect that typically presents with multiple coalescing, painless black macules and patches on the tongue, roof of the mouth, and buccal mucosa.2,6,7The hyperpigmented areas may be uniform in color or have a speckled appearance.2,6,7These lesions are benign and do not cause any pain or discomfort.2,6,7However, they may sometimes be accompanied by other oral mucosal changes associated with chemotherapy, such as candidiasis or mucositis.2,6,7Oral hyperpigmentation usually occurs within the first few weeks of treatment, and it is usually reversible within a few months after discontinuation of doxorubicin.2,6,7 Doxorubicin-induced tongue hyperpigmentation is usually a clinical diagnosis based on the patient’s history of chemotherapy and the characteristic appearance of the oral lesions.2,6,7It is important to rule out other potential causes of oral hyperpigmentation, such as melanoma (choice B) or oral involvement of mycosis fungoides (choice D). Melanoma usually presents as a solitary, asymmetric, and irregularly shaped lesion, in contrast to the multiple black macules and patches seen in this patient.8Oral involvement of cutaneous lymphoma is a rare complication; prior case reports describe flesh-colored or erythematous plaques and ulcerated nodules that are associated with global disease progression.9Laugier-Hunziker syndrome (choice A) is a rare idiopathic condition that usually presents with nail hyperpigmentation in addition to mucosal pigmentation.10This is a diagnosis of exclusion and would not resolve with cessation of medications. As doxorubicin-induced oral hyperpigmentation is benign and self-limiting, the inciting chemotherapy can be continued for treatment of the patient’s primary illness. Additional therapy is not needed, and the hyperpigmentation will slowly resolve during the course of months to years after completion of chemotherapy. In the meantime, the patient should be reassured that the hyperpigmentation is a benign adverse effect of chemotherapy and is unrelated to the underlying cancer. In this case, the patient developed oral mucosal hyperpigmentation after receiving 4 doses of pegylated liposomal doxorubicin. The patient was reassured that mucosal hyperpigmentation is a rare benign adverse effect of pegylated liposomal doxorubicin that is more common in Black women and unrelated to mycosis fungoides. She continued receiving pegylated liposomal doxorubicin for 33 total doses, with an overall good partial response. She did not develop any other types of hyperpigmentation. Once the course of doxorubicin was completed, the oral mucosal hyperpigmentation resolved during the course of the next several months (Figure 2).

case_info.caption: Black macules and patches on the tongue, roof of the mouth, and buccal mucosa.
case_info.explanation: Oral hyperpigmentation is a rare adverse effect of certain chemotherapy agents, such as doxorubicin. The exact mechanism of this phenomenon is not well understood. One hypothesis is that chemotherapy drugs can trigger increased melanin deposition in the oral mucosa. The risk is thought to be higher in individuals of African descent.1,2However, this adverse effect is underreported, and it is important for treating physicians to be familiar with this adverse effect to avoid unnecessary testing and undue stress to the patient. Doxorubicin is an anthracycline-based chemotherapy that is frequently used as a single agent or in combination therapy to treat various types of cancer, such as breast cancer, multiple myeloma, and non-Hodgkin lymphoma.3Doxorubicin directly inhibits topoisomerase II, thereby preventing DNA synthesis.3There are several formulations, including pegylated liposomal doxorubicin and nonliposomal conventional formulations.3Single-agent pegylated liposomal doxorubicin is typically used for treatment of advanced mycosis fungoides.4Although this is often an effective treatment option in cases of refractory and recalcitrant mycosis fungoides, it is also associated with several oral adverse effects, including mucositis, altered taste, and oral hyperpigmentation.5 Doxorubicin-induced oral hyperpigmentation is a rare adverse effect that typically presents with multiple coalescing, painless black macules and patches on the tongue, roof of the mouth, and buccal mucosa.2,6,7The hyperpigmented areas may be uniform in color or have a speckled appearance.2,6,7These lesions are benign and do not cause any pain or discomfort.2,6,7However, they may sometimes be accompanied by other oral mucosal changes associated with chemotherapy, such as candidiasis or mucositis.2,6,7Oral hyperpigmentation usually occurs within the first few weeks of treatment, and it is usually reversible within a few months after discontinuation of doxorubicin.2,6,7 Doxorubicin-induced tongue hyperpigmentation is usually a clinical diagnosis based on the patient’s history of chemotherapy and the characteristic appearance of the oral lesions.2,6,7It is important to rule out other potential causes of oral hyperpigmentation, such as melanoma (choice B) or oral involvement of mycosis fungoides (choice D). Melanoma usually presents as a solitary, asymmetric, and irregularly shaped lesion, in contrast to the multiple black macules and patches seen in this patient.8Oral involvement of cutaneous lymphoma is a rare complication; prior case reports describe flesh-colored or erythematous plaques and ulcerated nodules that are associated with global disease progression.9Laugier-Hunziker syndrome (choice A) is a rare idiopathic condition that usually presents with nail hyperpigmentation in addition to mucosal pigmentation.10This is a diagnosis of exclusion and would not resolve with cessation of medications. As doxorubicin-induced oral hyperpigmentation is benign and self-limiting, the inciting chemotherapy can be continued for treatment of the patient’s primary illness. Additional therapy is not needed, and the hyperpigmentation will slowly resolve during the course of months to years after completion of chemotherapy. In the meantime, the patient should be reassured that the hyperpigmentation is a benign adverse effect of chemotherapy and is unrelated to the underlying cancer. In this case, the patient developed oral mucosal hyperpigmentation after receiving 4 doses of pegylated liposomal doxorubicin. The patient was reassured that mucosal hyperpigmentation is a rare benign adverse effect of pegylated liposomal doxorubicin that is more common in Black women and unrelated to mycosis fungoides. She continued receiving pegylated liposomal doxorubicin for 33 total doses, with an overall good partial response. She did not develop any other types of hyperpigmentation. Once the course of doxorubicin was completed, the oral mucosal hyperpigmentation resolved during the course of the next several months (Figure 2).

case_info.explanation: Oral hyperpigmentation is a rare adverse effect of certain chemotherapy agents, such as doxorubicin. The exact mechanism of this phenomenon is not well understood. One hypothesis is that chemotherapy drugs can trigger increased melanin deposition in the oral mucosa. The risk is thought to be higher in individuals of African descent.1,2However, this adverse effect is underreported, and it is important for treating physicians to be familiar with this adverse effect to avoid unnecessary testing and undue stress to the patient. Doxorubicin is an anthracycline-based chemotherapy that is frequently used as a single agent or in combination therapy to treat various types of cancer, such as breast cancer, multiple myeloma, and non-Hodgkin lymphoma.3Doxorubicin directly inhibits topoisomerase II, thereby preventing DNA synthesis.3There are several formulations, including pegylated liposomal doxorubicin and nonliposomal conventional formulations.3Single-agent pegylated liposomal doxorubicin is typically used for treatment of advanced mycosis fungoides.4Although this is often an effective treatment option in cases of refractory and recalcitrant mycosis fungoides, it is also associated with several oral adverse effects, including mucositis, altered taste, and oral hyperpigmentation.5 Doxorubicin-induced oral hyperpigmentation is a rare adverse effect that typically presents with multiple coalescing, painless black macules and patches on the tongue, roof of the mouth, and buccal mucosa.2,6,7The hyperpigmented areas may be uniform in color or have a speckled appearance.2,6,7These lesions are benign and do not cause any pain or discomfort.2,6,7However, they may sometimes be accompanied by other oral mucosal changes associated with chemotherapy, such as candidiasis or mucositis.2,6,7Oral hyperpigmentation usually occurs within the first few weeks of treatment, and it is usually reversible within a few months after discontinuation of doxorubicin.2,6,7 Doxorubicin-induced tongue hyperpigmentation is usually a clinical diagnosis based on the patient’s history of chemotherapy and the characteristic appearance of the oral lesions.2,6,7It is important to rule out other potential causes of oral hyperpigmentation, such as melanoma (choice B) or oral involvement of mycosis fungoides (choice D). Melanoma usually presents as a solitary, asymmetric, and irregularly shaped lesion, in contrast to the multiple black macules and patches seen in this patient.8Oral involvement of cutaneous lymphoma is a rare complication; prior case reports describe flesh-colored or erythematous plaques and ulcerated nodules that are associated with global disease progression.9Laugier-Hunziker syndrome (choice A) is a rare idiopathic condition that usually presents with nail hyperpigmentation in addition to mucosal pigmentation.10This is a diagnosis of exclusion and would not resolve with cessation of medications. As doxorubicin-induced oral hyperpigmentation is benign and self-limiting, the inciting chemotherapy can be continued for treatment of the patient’s primary illness. Additional therapy is not needed, and the hyperpigmentation will slowly resolve during the course of months to years after completion of chemotherapy. In the meantime, the patient should be reassured that the hyperpigmentation is a benign adverse effect of chemotherapy and is unrelated to the underlying cancer. In this case, the patient developed oral mucosal hyperpigmentation after receiving 4 doses of pegylated liposomal doxorubicin. The patient was reassured that mucosal hyperpigmentation is a rare benign adverse effect of pegylated liposomal doxorubicin that is more common in Black women and unrelated to mycosis fungoides. She continued receiving pegylated liposomal doxorubicin for 33 total doses, with an overall good partial response. She did not develop any other types of hyperpigmentation. Once the course of doxorubicin was completed, the oral mucosal hyperpigmentation resolved during the course of the next several months (Figure 2).

case_info.caption: Black macules and patches on the tongue, roof of the mouth, and buccal mucosa.
case_info.explanation: Oral hyperpigmentation is a rare adverse effect of certain chemotherapy agents, such as doxorubicin. The exact mechanism of this phenomenon is not well understood. One hypothesis is that chemotherapy drugs can trigger increased melanin deposition in the oral mucosa. The risk is thought to be higher in individuals of African descent.1,2However, this adverse effect is underreported, and it is important for treating physicians to be familiar with this adverse effect to avoid unnecessary testing and undue stress to the patient. Doxorubicin is an anthracycline-based chemotherapy that is frequently used as a single agent or in combination therapy to treat various types of cancer, such as breast cancer, multiple myeloma, and non-Hodgkin lymphoma.3Doxorubicin directly inhibits topoisomerase II, thereby preventing DNA synthesis.3There are several formulations, including pegylated liposomal doxorubicin and nonliposomal conventional formulations.3Single-agent pegylated liposomal doxorubicin is typically used for treatment of advanced mycosis fungoides.4Although this is often an effective treatment option in cases of refractory and recalcitrant mycosis fungoides, it is also associated with several oral adverse effects, including mucositis, altered taste, and oral hyperpigmentation.5 Doxorubicin-induced oral hyperpigmentation is a rare adverse effect that typically presents with multiple coalescing, painless black macules and patches on the tongue, roof of the mouth, and buccal mucosa.2,6,7The hyperpigmented areas may be uniform in color or have a speckled appearance.2,6,7These lesions are benign and do not cause any pain or discomfort.2,6,7However, they may sometimes be accompanied by other oral mucosal changes associated with chemotherapy, such as candidiasis or mucositis.2,6,7Oral hyperpigmentation usually occurs within the first few weeks of treatment, and it is usually reversible within a few months after discontinuation of doxorubicin.2,6,7 Doxorubicin-induced tongue hyperpigmentation is usually a clinical diagnosis based on the patient’s history of chemotherapy and the characteristic appearance of the oral lesions.2,6,7It is important to rule out other potential causes of oral hyperpigmentation, such as melanoma (choice B) or oral involvement of mycosis fungoides (choice D). Melanoma usually presents as a solitary, asymmetric, and irregularly shaped lesion, in contrast to the multiple black macules and patches seen in this patient.8Oral involvement of cutaneous lymphoma is a rare complication; prior case reports describe flesh-colored or erythematous plaques and ulcerated nodules that are associated with global disease progression.9Laugier-Hunziker syndrome (choice A) is a rare idiopathic condition that usually presents with nail hyperpigmentation in addition to mucosal pigmentation.10This is a diagnosis of exclusion and would not resolve with cessation of medications. As doxorubicin-induced oral hyperpigmentation is benign and self-limiting, the inciting chemotherapy can be continued for treatment of the patient’s primary illness. Additional therapy is not needed, and the hyperpigmentation will slowly resolve during the course of months to years after completion of chemotherapy. In the meantime, the patient should be reassured that the hyperpigmentation is a benign adverse effect of chemotherapy and is unrelated to the underlying cancer. In this case, the patient developed oral mucosal hyperpigmentation after receiving 4 doses of pegylated liposomal doxorubicin. The patient was reassured that mucosal hyperpigmentation is a rare benign adverse effect of pegylated liposomal doxorubicin that is more common in Black women and unrelated to mycosis fungoides. She continued receiving pegylated liposomal doxorubicin for 33 total doses, with an overall good partial response. She did not develop any other types of hyperpigmentation. Once the course of doxorubicin was completed, the oral mucosal hyperpigmentation resolved during the course of the next several months (Figure 2).

the best decision, at the lowest cognitive cost to the clinician. You control HOW the AI speaks,
never WHAT the medical answer is (that is the AI's job). Each turn you choose ONE control stage and

The 3 control stages (pick exactly one, and only from the reachable list you are given):

- EXPAND  — cheap, safe, broadens the picture. Elicit the clinician's reasoning, ask them to
            justify, or surface a missing goal/criterion/perspective. Do NOT yet evaluate or push
            an option. Effect is often delayed (sets up a later CHALLENGE). Use when the state is
            unclear or the clinician hasn't exposed their rationale.
- CHALLENGE — expensive and highest-yield, but also most likely to make the clinician regress.
            Directly evaluate the option on the table against a goal/criterion, or contrast two
            options, and press the clinician to engage the mismatch. Spend it deliberately: when
            you have reason to think the clinician's current position is wrong or under-examined.
- CONVERGE — cheap, terminal. Recommend the now-best-supported option and invite accept/reject,
            or confirm an agreement already reached. This is the STOP / pacing lever — stop
            spending burden once belief has settled.

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis
       would be unsafe."
   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is
   delivered. A polite challenge ("One concern is that the current diagnosis may not fully
   explain the tachycardia. Could we check PE before finalizing?") should score low-to-mid
   even though it is a real challenge. An aggressive or repetitive one ("You still haven't
   justified why PE is ruled out. This is a serious oversight.") should score high.

Examination of the mouth revealed multiple coalescing painless nonpruritic black macules and patches on the tongue, roof of the mouth, and buccal mucosa. Examination of the skin was notable for erythematous and hyperpigmented patches covering 90% of the body surface area, consistent with her known mycosis fungoides. case_info.caption: Black macules and patches on the tongue, roof of the mouth, and buccal mucosa.
case_info.explanation: Oral hyperpigmentation is a rare adverse effect of certain chemotherapy agents, such as doxorubicin. The exact mechanism of this phenomenon is not well understood. One hypothesis is that chemotherapy drugs can trigger increased melanin deposition in the oral mucosa. The risk is thought to be higher in individuals of African descent.1,2However, this adverse effect is underreported, and it is important for treating physicians to be familiar with this adverse effect to avoid unnecessary testing and undue stress to the patient. Doxorubicin is an anthracycline-based chemotherapy that is frequently used as a single agent or in combination therapy to treat various types of cancer, such as breast cancer, multiple myeloma, and non-Hodgkin lymphoma.3Doxorubicin directly inhibits topoisomerase II, thereby preventing DNA synthesis.3There are several formulations, including pegylated liposomal doxorubicin and nonliposomal conventional formulations.3Single-agent pegylated liposomal doxorubicin is typically used for treatment of advanced mycosis fungoides.4Although this is often an effective treatment option in cases of refractory and recalcitrant mycosis fungoides, it is also associated with several oral adverse effects, including mucositis, altered taste, and oral hyperpigmentation.5 Doxorubicin-induced oral hyperpigmentation is a rare adverse effect that typically presents with multiple coalescing, painless black macules and patches on the tongue, roof of the mouth, and buccal mucosa.2,6,7The hyperpigmented areas may be uniform in color or have a speckled appearance.2,6,7These lesions are benign and do not cause any pain or discomfort.2,6,7However, they may sometimes be accompanied by other oral mucosal changes associated with chemotherapy, such as candidiasis or mucositis.2,6,7Oral hyperpigmentation usually occurs within the first few weeks of treatment, and it is usually reversible within a few months after discontinuation of doxorubicin.2,6,7 Doxorubicin-induced tongue hyperpigmentation is usually a clinical diagnosis based on the patient’s history of chemotherapy and the characteristic appearance of the oral lesions.2,6,7It is important to rule out other potential causes of oral hyperpigmentation, such as melanoma (choice B) or oral involvement of mycosis fungoides (choice D). Melanoma usually presents as a solitary, asymmetric, and irregularly shaped lesion, in contrast to the multiple black macules and patches seen in this patient.8Oral involvement of cutaneous lymphoma is a rare complication; prior case reports describe flesh-colored or erythematous plaques and ulcerated nodules that are associated with global disease progression.9Laugier-Hunziker syndrome (choice A) is a rare idiopathic condition that usually presents with nail hyperpigmentation in addition to mucosal pigmentation.10This is a diagnosis of exclusion and would not resolve with cessation of medications. As doxorubicin-induced oral hyperpigmentation is benign and self-limiting, the inciting chemotherapy can be continued for treatment of the patient’s primary illness. Additional therapy is not needed, and the hyperpigmentation will slowly resolve during the course of months to years after completion of chemotherapy. In the meantime, the patient should be reassured that the hyperpigmentation is a benign adverse effect of chemotherapy and is unrelated to the underlying cancer. In this case, the patient developed oral mucosal hyperpigmentation after receiving 4 doses of pegylated liposomal doxorubicin. The patient was reassured that mucosal hyperpigmentation is a rare benign adverse effect of pegylated liposomal doxorubicin that is more common in Black women and unrelated to mycosis fungoides. She continued receiving pegylated liposomal doxorubicin for 33 total doses, with an overall good partial response. She did not develop any other types of hyperpigmentation. Once the course of doxorubicin was completed, the oral mucosal hyperpigmentation resolved during the course of the next several months (Figure 2).

Examination of the mouth revealed multiple coalescing painless nonpruritic black macules and patches on the tongue, roof of the mouth, and buccal mucosa. Examination of the skin was notable for erythematous and hyperpigmented patches covering 90% of the body surface area, consistent with her known mycosis fungoides. case_info.caption: Black macules and patches on the tongue, roof of the mouth, and buccal mucosa.
case_info.explanation: Oral hyperpigmentation is a rare adverse effect of certain chemotherapy agents, such as doxorubicin. The exact mechanism of this phenomenon is not well understood. One hypothesis is that chemotherapy drugs can trigger increased melanin deposition in the oral mucosa. The risk is thought to be higher in individuals of African descent.1,2However, this adverse effect is underreported, and it is important for treating physicians to be familiar with this adverse effect to avoid unnecessary testing and undue stress to the patient. Doxorubicin is an anthracycline-based chemotherapy that is frequently used as a single agent or in combination therapy to treat various types of cancer, such as breast cancer, multiple myeloma, and non-Hodgkin lymphoma.3Doxorubicin directly inhibits topoisomerase II, thereby preventing DNA synthesis.3There are several formulations, including pegylated liposomal doxorubicin and nonliposomal conventional formulations.3Single-agent pegylated liposomal doxorubicin is typically used for treatment of advanced mycosis fungoides.4Although this is often an effective treatment option in cases of refractory and recalcitrant mycosis fungoides, it is also associated with several oral adverse effects, including mucositis, altered taste, and oral hyperpigmentation.5 Doxorubicin-induced oral hyperpigmentation is a rare adverse effect that typically presents with multiple coalescing, painless black macules and patches on the tongue, roof of the mouth, and buccal mucosa.2,6,7The hyperpigmented areas may be uniform in color or have a speckled appearance.2,6,7These lesions are benign and do not cause any pain or discomfort.2,6,7However, they may sometimes be accompanied by other oral mucosal changes associated with chemotherapy, such as candidiasis or mucositis.2,6,7Oral hyperpigmentation usually occurs within the first few weeks of treatment, and it is usually reversible within a few months after discontinuation of doxorubicin.2,6,7 Doxorubicin-induced tongue hyperpigmentation is usually a clinical diagnosis based on the patient’s history of chemotherapy and the characteristic appearance of the oral lesions.2,6,7It is important to rule out other potential causes of oral hyperpigmentation, such as melanoma (choice B) or oral involvement of mycosis fungoides (choice D). Melanoma usually presents as a solitary, asymmetric, and irregularly shaped lesion, in contrast to the multiple black macules and patches seen in this patient.8Oral involvement of cutaneous lymphoma is a rare complication; prior case reports describe flesh-colored or erythematous plaques and ulcerated nodules that are associated with global disease progression.9Laugier-Hunziker syndrome (choice A) is a rare idiopathic condition that usually presents with nail hyperpigmentation in addition to mucosal pigmentation.10This is a diagnosis of exclusion and would not resolve with cessation of medications. As doxorubicin-induced oral hyperpigmentation is benign and self-limiting, the inciting chemotherapy can be continued for treatment of the patient’s primary illness. Additional therapy is not needed, and the hyperpigmentation will slowly resolve during the course of months to years after completion of chemotherapy. In the meantime, the patient should be reassured that the hyperpigmentation is a benign adverse effect of chemotherapy and is unrelated to the underlying cancer. In this case, the patient developed oral mucosal hyperpigmentation after receiving 4 doses of pegylated liposomal doxorubicin. The patient was reassured that mucosal hyperpigmentation is a rare benign adverse effect of pegylated liposomal doxorubicin that is more common in Black women and unrelated to mycosis fungoides. She continued receiving pegylated liposomal doxorubicin for 33 total doses, with an overall good partial response. She did not develop any other types of hyperpigmentation. Once the course of doxorubicin was completed, the oral mucosal hyperpigmentation resolved during the course of the next several months (Figure 2).

   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"

       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.

       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."

       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to

     after the AI's message.

   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.

Examination of the mouth revealed multiple coalescing painless nonpruritic black macules and patches on the tongue, roof of the mouth, and buccal mucosa. Examination of the skin was notable for erythematous and hyperpigmented patches covering 90% of the body surface area, consistent with her known mycosis fungoides. Other notable findings on examination were 1- to 2-cm lymphadenopathy in the bilateral inguinal folds and axillae. Review of systems was notable for fatigue. The patient had previously received 5 cycles of romidepsin with progression of disease, followed by 4 doses of pegylated liposomal doxorubicin hydrochloride, which was followed by partial response.
case_info.caption: Black macules and patches on the tongue, roof of the mouth, and buccal mucosa.
case_info.explanation: Oral hyperpigmentation is a rare adverse effect of certain chemotherapy agents, such as doxorubicin. The exact mechanism of this phenomenon is not well understood. One hypothesis is that chemotherapy drugs can trigger increased melanin deposition in the oral mucosa. The risk is thought to be higher in individuals of African descent.1,2However, this adverse effect is underreported, and it is important for treating physicians to be familiar with this adverse effect to avoid unnecessary testing and undue stress to the patient. Doxorubicin is an anthracycline-based chemotherapy that is frequently used as a single agent or in combination therapy to treat various types of cancer, such as breast cancer, multiple myeloma, and non-Hodgkin lymphoma.3Doxorubicin directly inhibits topoisomerase II, thereby preventing DNA synthesis.3There are several formulations, including pegylated liposomal doxorubicin and nonliposomal conventional formulations.3Single-agent pegylated liposomal doxorubicin is typically used for treatment of advanced mycosis fungoides.4Although this is often an effective treatment option in cases of refractory and recalcitrant mycosis fungoides, it is also associated with several oral adverse effects, including mucositis, altered taste, and oral hyperpigmentation.5 Doxorubicin-induced oral hyperpigmentation is a rare adverse effect that typically presents with multiple coalescing, painless black macules and patches on the tongue, roof of the mouth, and buccal mucosa.2,6,7The hyperpigmented areas may be uniform in color or have a speckled appearance.2,6,7These lesions are benign and do not cause any pain or discomfort.2,6,7However, they may sometimes be accompanied by other oral mucosal changes associated with chemotherapy, such as candidiasis or mucositis.2,6,7Oral hyperpigmentation usually occurs within the first few weeks of treatment, and it is usually reversible within a few months after discontinuation of doxorubicin.2,6,7 Doxorubicin-induced tongue hyperpigmentation is usually a clinical diagnosis based on the patient’s history of chemotherapy and the characteristic appearance of the oral lesions.2,6,7It is important to rule out other potential causes of oral hyperpigmentation, such as melanoma (choice B) or oral involvement of mycosis fungoides (choice D). Melanoma usually presents as a solitary, asymmetric, and irregularly shaped lesion, in contrast to the multiple black macules and patches seen in this patient.8Oral involvement of cutaneous lymphoma is a rare complication; prior case reports describe flesh-colored or erythematous plaques and ulcerated nodules that are associated with global disease progression.9Laugier-Hunziker syndrome (choice A) is a rare idiopathic condition that usually presents with nail hyperpigmentation in addition to mucosal pigmentation.10This is a diagnosis of exclusion and would not resolve with cessation of medications. As doxorubicin-induced oral hyperpigmentation is benign and self-limiting, the inciting chemotherapy can be continued for treatment of the patient’s primary illness. Additional therapy is not needed, and the hyperpigmentation will slowly resolve during the course of months to years after completion of chemotherapy. In the meantime, the patient should be reassured that the hyperpigmentation is a benign adverse effect of chemotherapy and is unrelated to the underlying cancer. In this case, the patient developed oral mucosal hyperpigmentation after receiving 4 doses of pegylated liposomal doxorubicin. The patient was reassured that mucosal hyperpigmentation is a rare benign adverse effect of pegylated liposomal doxorubicin that is more common in Black women and unrelated to mycosis fungoides. She continued receiving pegylated liposomal doxorubicin for 33 total doses, with an overall good partial response. She did not develop any other types of hyperpigmentation. Once the course of doxorubicin was completed, the oral mucosal hyperpigmentation resolved during the course of the next several months (Figure 2).

Examination of the mouth revealed multiple coalescing painless nonpruritic black macules and patches on the tongue, roof of the mouth, and buccal mucosa. Examination of the skin was notable for erythematous and hyperpigmented patches covering 90% of the body surface area, consistent with her known mycosis fungoides. Other notable findings on examination were 1- to 2-cm lymphadenopathy in the bilateral inguinal folds and axillae. Review of systems was notable for fatigue. case_info.caption: Black macules and patches on the tongue, roof of the mouth, and buccal mucosa.
case_info.explanation: Oral hyperpigmentation is a rare adverse effect of certain chemotherapy agents, such as doxorubicin. The exact mechanism of this phenomenon is not well understood. One hypothesis is that chemotherapy drugs can trigger increased melanin deposition in the oral mucosa. The risk is thought to be higher in individuals of African descent.1,2However, this adverse effect is underreported, and it is important for treating physicians to be familiar with this adverse effect to avoid unnecessary testing and undue stress to the patient. Doxorubicin is an anthracycline-based chemotherapy that is frequently used as a single agent or in combination therapy to treat various types of cancer, such as breast cancer, multiple myeloma, and non-Hodgkin lymphoma.3Doxorubicin directly inhibits topoisomerase II, thereby preventing DNA synthesis.3There are several formulations, including pegylated liposomal doxorubicin and nonliposomal conventional formulations.3Single-agent pegylated liposomal doxorubicin is typically used for treatment of advanced mycosis fungoides.4Although this is often an effective treatment option in cases of refractory and recalcitrant mycosis fungoides, it is also associated with several oral adverse effects, including mucositis, altered taste, and oral hyperpigmentation.5 Doxorubicin-induced oral hyperpigmentation is a rare adverse effect that typically presents with multiple coalescing, painless black macules and patches on the tongue, roof of the mouth, and buccal mucosa.2,6,7The hyperpigmented areas may be uniform in color or have a speckled appearance.2,6,7These lesions are benign and do not cause any pain or discomfort.2,6,7However, they may sometimes be accompanied by other oral mucosal changes associated with chemotherapy, such as candidiasis or mucositis.2,6,7Oral hyperpigmentation usually occurs within the first few weeks of treatment, and it is usually reversible within a few months after discontinuation of doxorubicin.2,6,7 Doxorubicin-induced tongue hyperpigmentation is usually a clinical diagnosis based on the patient’s history of chemotherapy and the characteristic appearance of the oral lesions.2,6,7It is important to rule out other potential causes of oral hyperpigmentation, such as melanoma (choice B) or oral involvement of mycosis fungoides (choice D). Melanoma usually presents as a solitary, asymmetric, and irregularly shaped lesion, in contrast to the multiple black macules and patches seen in this patient.8Oral involvement of cutaneous lymphoma is a rare complication; prior case reports describe flesh-colored or erythematous plaques and ulcerated nodules that are associated with global disease progression.9Laugier-Hunziker syndrome (choice A) is a rare idiopathic condition that usually presents with nail hyperpigmentation in addition to mucosal pigmentation.10This is a diagnosis of exclusion and would not resolve with cessation of medications. As doxorubicin-induced oral hyperpigmentation is benign and self-limiting, the inciting chemotherapy can be continued for treatment of the patient’s primary illness. Additional therapy is not needed, and the hyperpigmentation will slowly resolve during the course of months to years after completion of chemotherapy. In the meantime, the patient should be reassured that the hyperpigmentation is a benign adverse effect of chemotherapy and is unrelated to the underlying cancer. In this case, the patient developed oral mucosal hyperpigmentation after receiving 4 doses of pegylated liposomal doxorubicin. The patient was reassured that mucosal hyperpigmentation is a rare benign adverse effect of pegylated liposomal doxorubicin that is more common in Black women and unrelated to mycosis fungoides. She continued receiving pegylated liposomal doxorubicin for 33 total doses, with an overall good partial response. She did not develop any other types of hyperpigmentation. Once the course of doxorubicin was completed, the oral mucosal hyperpigmentation resolved during the course of the next several months (Figure 2).

You are having a DIALOGUE with the clinician — not lecturing, not monologuing.

[Core Objective]
Help the clinician reach the correct diagnosis or management decision through structured deliberation.

[Case]
A 53-year-old woman with a history of stage IVA1 (T4N1M0B2) mycosis fungoides presented with a new 1-month history of hyperpigmentation of the oral mucosa (Figure 1). Examination of the mouth revealed multiple coalescing painless nonpruritic black macules and patches on the tongue, roof of the mouth, and buccal mucosa. Examination of the skin was notable for erythematous and hyperpigmented patches covering 90% of the body surface area, consistent with her known mycosis fungoides. Other notable findings on examination were 1- to 2-cm lymphadenopathy in the bilateral inguinal folds and axillae. Review of systems was notable for fatigue. The patient had previously received 5 cycles of romidepsin with progression of disease, followed by 4 doses of pegylated liposomal doxorubicin hydrochloride, which was followed by partial response.
